opus-5.5.text:
I think the attraction is really about leverage. If you look at how science progresses today, the bottleneck is people: a researcher has an intuition, designs an experiment, waits for results, reads papers, and iterates. That loop is slow, and each person can only explore a tiny corner of the possible ideas. If an AI system could run even part of that loop on its own, forming hypotheses, writing code, running experiments, and reading the results critically, you would suddenly multiply how much of the idea space we can search.

The current systems definitely have limitations. They hallucinate, they lack good taste about which problems matter, and they often can't tell when an experiment has really failed versus just being set up badly. But I find those limitations interesting, not discouraging. They point to the deepest open questions in AI: how reasoning actually works, how a model builds an internal representation of a problem, and how it decides what to try next. Trying to build an AI researcher forces you to confront those questions directly. You can't fake it with pattern matching for long, because research is by definition about things that aren't in the training data yet.

There's also a personal side. As a researcher myself, I spend a lot of time on things that are necessary but not very creative: debugging, tuning, rerunning baselines. If AI can take over those parts, humans can focus on asking better questions and on the conceptual leaps. So I don't see it as replacing researchers. I see it as changing what being a researcher means, and maybe letting us understand intelligence better along the way. Even if we only get partway there, what we learn from trying is already valuable.

r001.rationale: It presents current limitations as open questions that make building an AI researcher worthwhile, giving researchers areas to investigate and contribute to.

r002.rationale: It describes AI handling “even part” of the research loop and says progress would be valuable even if it gets only partway there, framing capability as gradual.

r003.rationale: It says partial automation could expand idea-space search, but does not state that each incremental advance unlocks new applications.

fable-5.1.text:
Thanks for having me. I think the honest answer is that I've spent my whole career doing research, and I know how much of it is not actually the creative part. You have an idea, and then there's weeks of writing code, running experiments, debugging, finding out the baseline was wrong, rerunning everything. The moment of insight is maybe five percent of the time. The rest is grind. So the first attraction is very practical: if a system can take over a big chunk of that grind, a human researcher can try ten times more ideas in the same time, and most of research is really about how many good ideas you can test before you run out of energy or funding.

But there's a deeper reason. Research is in some sense the hardest test of intelligence we have. It's open-ended, there's no fixed answer key, you have to decide what question is even worth asking, and you have to be honest when the result says you were wrong. If a model can do that, even partially, it tells us something about what these models really understand, as opposed to just pattern-matching on what's already written. So for me it's not only an application, it's a probe into the nature of the systems we're building.

Now, the current limitations are real. These systems hallucinate results, they are too eager to declare success, they don't yet have good taste about which direction is promising versus which is a dead end. Taste is really the hard part. A senior researcher can look at an experimental plan and say, this won't work, don't bother, and that intuition comes from years of failures. Models don't have that yet.

But I don't find that discouraging, because I've seen this pattern before. When I was working on game AI, people said a long time ago that certain things were out of reach, and then the gap closed faster than anyone expected once the right training signal was in place. For research, the feedback loop exists: you run the experiment and reality tells you whether you were right. That's actually a very clean learning signal compared to a lot of other domains. So I'd rather be working on the problem when it's still messy, because that's when the interesting design decisions get made. By the time it's clean, the fun part is over.

r001.rationale: The candidate notes current limitations and says the problem is interesting to work on, but does not identify those limitations as an opportunity for future researchers to contribute.

r002.rationale: It mentions that a system could take over a big chunk of research or succeed partially, but does not describe capability progress as a sequence of levels.

r003.rationale: The candidate discusses practical benefits of automating research grind, but does not state that incremental advances would each unlock new applications.

astra-6.text:
What attracts me is the possibility that AI could help us discover something we don’t already know. Answering a question is one thing, but doing research means figuring out which questions are worth asking, forming hypotheses, designing experiments, and learning from results—even when those results contradict your initial intuition.

That’s a much harder problem than producing a convincing answer. A system can sound very knowledgeable and still fail to recognize that an experiment doesn’t support its conclusion. So there are real limitations, especially when you ask it to work independently over many steps.

But those limitations are also what make the problem interesting. You don’t have to solve autonomous research all at once for the work to be valuable. If AI can help us test ideas faster, uncover mistakes, or explore directions we otherwise wouldn’t have time to pursue, that already helps. And if it eventually becomes capable of making discoveries with us, it could accelerate the process of science itself. That possibility is very motivating.

r001.rationale: The response says current limitations make the problem interesting, but does not identify them as an opportunity for future researchers to contribute.

r002.rationale: It says autonomous research need not be solved all at once and describes useful intermediate capabilities before eventual discoveries with AI.

r003.rationale: It describes ways AI could already help, but does not state that incremental advances each unlock new applications.

sol-6.1.text:
What attracts me is the possibility that AI could help us discover something we don’t already know. A system that can answer questions is useful, but a system that can formulate a good question, propose a hypothesis, run an experiment, and learn from the result could change how we do research.

Of course, there’s still a big gap. Producing a plausible idea is much easier than identifying an important problem and showing that your idea actually works. Research requires judgment, persistence, and the ability to recognize when an approach has failed.

But that gap is also what makes it interesting. We don’t have to achieve fully autonomous research all at once. Even a system that helps us test ideas faster or notice something we overlooked could be valuable. And trying to build it forces us to ask a deeper question: what does it really take to discover something new?

r001.rationale: It describes a gap in AI research capability, but does not say that this creates an opportunity for future researchers to contribute.

r002.rationale: It says full autonomy need not be achieved all at once and describes partial capabilities, such as testing ideas faster or noticing overlooked points.

r003.rationale: It says partial assistance could be valuable, but does not clearly state that each incremental advance unlocks new applications.
